claims.text: Adding a modest amount of aluminum to a refractory high-entropy alloy will improve its high-temperature oxygen resistance.
The improvement from aluminum addition will result from formation of a continuous protective alumina scale.
W-Ta-V-Cr is a refractory high-entropy alloy system.
The untreated W-Ta-V-Cr-like alloy does not form a protective oxide layer at extreme temperatures.
The proposed effect should operate in air or another oxygen-rich atmosphere at 1000-1200°C for exposures such as 50 hours.
Aluminum will segregate to the alloy surface during high-temperature exposure.
Surface aluminum will oxidize preferentially to form alumina.
The resulting alumina scale will be slow-growing and dense.
A continuous alumina scale will impede oxygen penetration into the underlying alloy.
Impeded oxygen penetration will reduce oxidation of the underlying refractory HEA.
The aluminum-modified alloy will develop a significantly thinner oxide scale than the untreated alloy.
The aluminum-modified alloy will have lower oxidation kinetics than the untreated alloy.
Reduced oxidation will enhance mechanical stability during extreme-temperature exposure.
Untreated refractory HEAs form thicker, less protective oxide scales under comparable high-temperature, oxygen-rich conditions.
Too little aluminum may fail to produce an effective protective oxide layer.
Too much aluminum may produce brittle intermetallic phases or non-protective oxide morphologies.
Alumina formation kinetics and adhesion are favorable in the approximate range of 1000-1200°C.
The magnitude of oxidation-resistance improvement is sensitive to aluminum concentration and processing route.
Long-term thermal cycling may affect the stability of the alumina layer.
